questions.q: What historical example does the lesson give of a disruptive quantum SDK version transition?
options: NumPy 1.x to 2.x
Qiskit's 0.x-series to 1.0 transition, which removed qiskit.execute() and restructured backend access
Python 2 to Python 3
pandas 1.0 release
questions.explain: The lesson cites Qiskit's 0.x to 1.0 transition -- which removed qiskit.execute() and restructured the transpiler and backend-access APIs -- as a concrete example of the kind of disruptive change that is comparatively rare in mature classical libraries like NumPy.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'silent break' from a 'loud break' when a quantum SDK updates?
options: A silent break only affects documentation, never code
A silent break still runs without error but changes numerical behavior, while a loud break raises an immediate error like AttributeError
A loud break only happens in Q#, never in Qiskit
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: Loud breaks remove or rename an API, so code fails immediately and visibly. Silent breaks are more dangerous: the API still runs, but something like a transpiler default changed, altering numerical results without any error being raised.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend exact pins (`==`) for quantum SDK dependencies rather than ranges (`>=`) as is common in many classical Python projects?
options: Because pip doesn't support ranges for quantum packages
Because quantum SDKs are mature enough that ranges are actually safer here
Because quantum SDKs change behavior, including silently, more frequently than typical mature classical libraries, so a range risks pulling in an incompatible or numerically different version
Exact pins are only a stylistic preference with no functional benefit
questions.explain: Because quantum SDKs churn (including silent numerical changes) more than mature classical libraries, the lesson recommends exact == pins plus a committed lockfile, rather than trusting a >= range to stay safe.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend committing a lockfile (e.g. uv.lock or poetry.lock) in addition to pinning versions in pyproject.toml?
options: A lockfile is purely optional documentation with no functional effect
Pinning qiskit==1.2.4 in pyproject.toml alone doesn't guarantee identical transitive dependencies (like rustworkx or symengine) across machines, which a lockfile does guarantee
Lockfiles replace the need for pyproject.toml entirely
Lockfiles are only needed for Q#, not Qiskit
questions.explain: Even with qiskit pinned exactly, its own transitive dependencies could still resolve differently on two machines without a lockfile, which can change transpiler behavior under the hood -- the lockfile fixes the entire resolved tree, not just the top-level pin.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend separate environments (e.g. qiskit-env/ and qsharp-env/) rather than installing Qiskit and Q#/QDK into one environment?
options: Because Microsoft prohibits installing Q# alongside any other SDK by license
Because the two ecosystems have different release cadences and dependency sets not designed to coexist cleanly in one environment
Because Python only allows one quantum package installed at a time
Because separate environments make circuits run faster
questions.explain: Qiskit and Q#/QDK have independent release cadences and dependency trees that aren't designed to coexist in a single environment, so the lesson recommends isolating them and connecting them through a backend-abstraction boundary (built in Chapter 3) instead.
